# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# Review of Varga & Holm: "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem" (Comment on the Halden Pilot)

Sections 1–5 are a valuable, mostly sound re-analysis. They show with data what could only be suspected from the Halden working paper. Sections 6–8 and the headline conclusion go well beyond what that re-analysis shows, and they handle the Varden evidence selectively.

## Arithmetic

Most figures check out:

| Figure | Check | Reported |
|---|---|---|
| Record-based output, scheduled hours | 95.1 / 0.8 = 1.189 | +18.9% |
| Hours ratio, 27 organisations | 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859 (−14.1%) | 0.859 |
| Manager output, actual hours | 98.4 / 0.859 = 1.146 | +14.6% |
| Hours ratio, 17 organisations | 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861 (−13.9%) | 0.861 |
| Record-based output, actual hours | 95.4 / 0.861 = 1.108 | +10.8% |
| Real revenue | 1.014 / 1.041 = 0.974 | −2.6% |
| Overstatement of hours reduction | 20 − 14.1 = 5.9 | "roughly six points" |

There are two problems.

**The hours decomposition in §3 doesn't add up.**
- Four 8-hour days is 32 scheduled hours.
- Adding 0.7 hours on each of four days (2.8 hours) and 1.6 hours on the day off gives 36.4 hours, not 34.6.
- Measuring "longer days" against baseline actual days (8.06 hours) gives about 36.6.
- Either the components or the 34.6 average is wrong. If the components are right, actual hours fell by only about 9–10%.
- This needs reconciling before publication.

**The novelty extrapolation in §6 is off.** Energy falls by 0.32 SD over three months and stands at 0.29 SD, so a linear trend reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten." This is minor next to the deeper problems with the extrapolation (see §2 below).

## 1. The abstract misdescribes the analysis

The abstract says that correcting "the first three" problems reduces the gain to 10.8%. The first three are attrition, the output measure and the hours denominator. Attrition is never corrected. Table 2 adjusts only output and hours, and only among surviving organisations.

The authors have the microdata and recommend analysing all enrolled organisations. They should do so themselves:
- Use whatever monthly indices exist for the seven organisations that withdrew after the schedule began.
- Otherwise, report bounds by imputing plausible outcomes for the withdrawn organisations.

Without that, attrition is a credible direction of bias, not a quantified correction.

## 2. The novelty argument ignores data the authors hold

- **The output trajectory is already in the microdata.** The Halden output index was collected monthly, so it can be tested directly whether output, not self-reported energy, declines over months 1–6. The time-tracking logs could likewise show whether hours creep back up. Neither analysis appears.
- **Energy is not output.** A linear extrapolation from two points is not evidence of decay to zero; the measure could just as easily plateau. And energy is a proxy whose link to productivity the comment assumes.
- **The comment applies its own evidence standard unevenly.** §7 rejects a seven-office correlation as a "post hoc account." §6 then rests a strong conclusion on a two-point trend in a secondary self-report measure.

## 3. "Entirely an artifact" is not supported, and is contradicted by the evidence the comment cites

- The authors' own corrected estimate leaves a gain of about 11%. Their only argument that this is spurious is the novelty claim.
- The comment treats Varden's counter stratum as "the most reliable finding in the literature." It omits Varden's case-processing stratum, which found +12.5% output per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4).
  - That result comes from randomisation, record-based output and timesheet hours.
  - Those are exactly the corrections this comment calls for.
  - It is strikingly close to the comment's own corrected 10.8%.
- Two independent sources, corrected for measurement and selection, converge on a gain of about 10–12% in work not tied to presence. That points towards a real effect in that kind of work, not an artifact.
- Novelty remains a fair caveat at nine months. Varden's 24-month follow-up will speak to it.
- Even a gain from removing idle time or meetings would be a real gain, not a measurement artifact. Calling it an artifact conflates "smaller than claimed" and "uncertain mechanism" with "not there."
- **The conclusion conflates per-employee and per-hour results.**
  - "Where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output" is a per-employee finding, and it is well supported.
  - It does not support the claim that per-hour gains are artifacts. Varden's counter stratum itself showed +6.7% per actual hour, though that may largely reflect higher staff utilisation as queues lengthen.

A defensible conclusion would say something like this: *published per-hour gains from voluntary pilots are overstated by roughly half; a residual gain of about 10–12% appears in work not tied to presence, corroborated by randomised evidence, though its durability is untested; and in coverage-bound work, output per employee falls.*

## 4. Section 7 misrepresents the Varden analysis

- **Varden did not claim a mechanism.** They said meetings "may account for part" of the gain, flagged the analysis as unregistered, noted that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism, and registered a confirmatory test.
- **"Selected for analysis after the results were known" is inaccurate.** The meeting data were collected in month six, at managers' request, before the nine-month results.
- **"A subgroup" is misleading.** The case-processing offices are a pre-specified randomisation stratum. What was post hoc was the measure, not the subgroup.

The comment's real point is that the evidence is weak. That is fair: the 95% CI on r = 0.71 with n = 7 runs from about −0.09 to 0.95. But "should not be cited as a mechanism" responds to a claim Varden did not make.

## 5. Methodological points on the re-analysis

- **Table 2 mixes subsets.** Its rows use 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations, so differences between rows combine the effect of each correction with differences in which organisations are included. Compute all four specifications on the same 17 organisations so each correction's effect is isolated.
- **No uncertainty is reported.** Tables 1 and 2 have no confidence intervals. With 17–27 organisations, the 10.8% estimate could be quite imprecise.
- **The records are not uniform, and not necessarily an unbiased benchmark.**
  - "Billable hours delivered" is partly an input measure. Using it as output pushes per-hour gains toward zero by construction.
  - "Tickets closed" can be gamed.
  - Report the manager–record gap by type of record.
- **The data note's caveat should appear in the abstract and conclusion.** The note correctly warns that the corrected estimates describe non-random subsets. The abstract and conclusion generalise from them anyway.
- **The attrition finding is a factual claim against the original authors.** The working paper says organisations withdrew "during the preparation phase." The microdata show seven of nine withdrew after the schedule began. Cite the specific variables (withdrawal dates and exit-form fields). Also note that only eight of nine exit reasons are accounted for.
- **The CPI deflator is approximate.** CPI is a rough deflator for business and non-profit revenue; producer or sector price indices would be better. The direction of the correction is clearly right.

## Overall

Sections 1–5 show the Halden headline is overstated:
- non-random attrition, now documented
- systematic manager inflation, of about 4 points in 19 of 23 organisations
- an hours denominator off by about 6 points
- real revenue down, not up
- per-hour figures that disguise a sectoral output loss

These are well-evidenced contributions.

The comment then turns "overstated by about half" into "entirely an artifact." To get there, it relies on an untested novelty extrapolation and leaves out the randomised result that best matches its own corrected estimate.

Recommendations:
- Correct the abstract.
- Run the monthly-trajectory and attrition-bounds analyses that the microdata permit.
- Engage with Varden's case-processing stratum.
- Replace "entirely an artifact" with a conclusion proportionate to the evidence.
